The genesis of the hard hematite ore deposits at Ely and Soudan on the Vermilion Range, Minnesota, U.S.A. (Fig. 1) has been disputed. Winchell and Winchell (1891) proposed that they are anamorphosed primary chemical sediments. Clements (1903) and Abbott (1907) proposed that iron-bearing groundwater solutions metasomatically replaced the primary iron-formation in structural troughs. Van Hise and Leith (1911) argued that groundwater leached and oxidized the primary iron-formation to form residual soft hematite deposits, which at Soudan were metamorphosed directly to hard hematite and at Ely were weathered to laterites and then metamorphosed. Royce (1942) also argued that meteoric solutions created residual soft hematite deposits, which were subsequently metamorphosed to hard hematite. They came from: the Republic Mine, Marquette Range; the Groveland Mine, Felch Mountain District; and along the Menominee Range. Standard paleomagnetic pro- cedures were used to study the samples. The Negaunee and Vulcan iron formations are thought to have been deposited as primary sediments of the hematite-banded and magnetite-banded oxide facies with chemical reinanent magnetization (CRM) during the Middle Animikie. During dynamic or thermal metamorphism, the primary remanence directions were modified causing them to be rotated into the bedding plane to yield directions that are random in declination but which are uniformly dis- tributed about the bedding plane in inclination. The metamorphism was likely associated with the Penokean orogeny during which the iron forma- tions were tightly folded and then thermally metamorphosed. Paleo- magnetism suggests that the iron formation at the Republic and Groveland Mines has been folded into synclines. The purpose of this study was to see if metamorphosed iron formation from three localities in northern Michigan (Fig. 1) has a similar remanence and if paleomagnetism would prove useful in studying the genesis of the concentrating iron deposits in the iron formation. The three iron formations are thought to be contemporaneous; they have been subjected to low-, intermediate-, and high-grade thermal metamorphism, and to moderate and intense dynamic metamorphism; and they are mined as concentrating iron ores at two of the localities. ng or postfolding grouping of remanence directions. However, their mean inclination is only 3.5 ø ----- 15 ø (s.d.) from the bedding plane and their declinations are randomly oriented as shown in Figure 5b which indicates a strong bias of the remanence direction to the bedding plane of the jaspilite ore. These jaspilite ore samples exhibit a moderate magnetic anisotropy as shown by the susceptibility differences measured along orthogonal axes. The measurements show that on average, the maximum susceptibility is at least 25 percent greater than the minimum susceptibility and approximately parallel to the bedding plane. The bias of the remanence direction to the bedding plane and the apparent anisotropy in the bedding plane suggest that the primary remanence direction has been modified and rotated into the bedding plane by metamorphism. section_candidates.excerpt: the largest (250 km2 ) of the islands forming the Cook Islands (Fig. 1). The island is rugged, numerous peaks rising over 500 m, but the highest point is only 650 m. The volcanic hills are surrounded by a narrow coastal strip of coral sand and other beach deposits, usually separated from the hills by an elongated swampy depression. The coastal strip, which consists in part of raised reef and beach material, supports most of the island's population and provides the greatest area of flat land. Marshall (1930) described the volcanic geology in some detail, but presented only a small locality map. He inferred an alternating sequence of basaltic and phonolitic eruptions. More recent work by Wood and Hay (1967), illustrated by a geological map, shows that the strongly dissected landforms still display the elements of the major volcanic structures-a large basaltic cone, with younger phonolitic eruptives occupying a caldera. The latest eruptions are considered to be probably as young as late Tertiary or early Pleistocene, like those of strongly dissected Oahu, Hawaiian Islands (McDougall, 1964; McDougall and Tarling, 1963). For one group of Jurassic sandstones from the Bayburt-GUmUshane region it proved to be very difficult to determine accurately the characteristic direc- tion of magnetization: the samples contained secondary magnetizations, concealing the ancient natural remanent magnetization (N.R.M.). The result is therefore regarded as unreliable. Fieldwork and sampling in northern and eastern Turkey was done in April 1965 and May 1966; nine groups of oriented samples were collected, varying in age from Permian to Tertiary. From these the Permian samples from Hazro (east of Diyarbakir), one group of Lower Cretaceous radiolarites and volcanics from Ergani and another group of Eocene volcanics near Bayburt contained only present-day local geomagnetic field directions; the results of five groups of Jurassic (from Bayburt), Cretaceous (from Niksar and GHmUshane) and Eocene age (GUmUshane and Tunceli) are presented here (summarized in Table II), and the results of some Oligocene Miocene volcanics will be published later. This mountain range lies immediately to the north of a great zone of dextral strike slip faults, together forming the North Anatolian faultzone, which runs from the Sea of Marmora to Lake Van and to Erzurum in eastern Turkey. of a great zone of dextral strike slip faults, together forming the North Anatolian faultzone, which runs from the Sea of Marmora to Lake Van and to Erzurum in eastern Turkey. Arni (1939) and Blumenthal (1964) described the Pontide chains as a mountain range with mainly Cretaceous sediments and volcanics around a few Paleozoic nuclei. The geology of the Giimiishane region (Fig.2) has been described recently by Zankl (1961), who paid special attention to the volcanics of Jurassic and Cretaceous age in a north-south cross-section through the eastern Pontides. Apart from various intrusive complexes, these volcanics consist of flows of basalt, trachy-andesite, dacite, spilite and rhyolite, intercalated between sediments, tuffs and agglomerates. The marine sedi- ments in this sequence (limestones, sandstones and marls) made it possible to attribute most of the volcanics to either the Jurassic or the Early Cretaceous or the Late Cretaceous-Eocene period and to establish their correct tectonical dip. Irving and Parry (1963) have shown, the directions of magnetization of some Carboniferous rocks from Australia are similar to those found in Australian Permian rocks. To avoid confusion they went so far as to propose that an independent magnetic chronology be set up. The basins here studied are particularly apposite to the paleomagnetic study of the Carboniferous-Permian boundary, for there are lithologies suitable for paleomag- netic work, well dated because of the economic importance of the included coals. This time interval is not particularly well known paleo- magnetically (see, however, Creer and others 1959; Everitt and Belshe, 1960; Nairn, 1960; Collinson and Nairn, 1960). Until recently it has been generally assumed that relative movements within a continental block are unimportant, and one of the major problems has been to understand the dispersion of virtual pole positions found for some periods, such as the Carboniferous. The growing aware- ness of rotation of presumed tectonic origin, even within a continental area (Black, 1964; Kotasek and Krs, 1965; Ashworth and Nairn, 1965; Watkins, 1964; Irving and Opdyke, 1965; Kawai and others, 1962; van Hilten, 1962), necessitates the study of relatively re- stricted areas between which there are differ- ences in tectonic develop

ky Brod (Rossitz-Bohmische Brod). The nearly flat-lying sediments arc practically un- disturbed except by faulting, more marked in the Plzeii basin than in the Kladno basin. This reflects renewed activity along older tectonic lines until as late as the Tertiary. Sedimenta- tion occurred with only minor breaks (sec Table 1) until the end of the Stcphanian, with a maximum in Westphalian D and Stephanian B. The presence of Permian rocks has some- times been assumed (for example, Dorn, 1966), but has not been proven (see Havlena, 1966). The sedimentary rocks are predominantly continental sandstones and shales with eco- nomically important coal scams and some kaolin deposits. Volcanic rocks, porphyries, mclaphyres and tufls are known here as well as m the Inner Sudetic basin, and these may, as there, be related to weak movements of the Asturic phase. This alternation has been attributed to climatic variation, but may equally well be due to fluctuating ground-water level consequent upon minor uplifts or depres- sions of tectonic origin, or to sea-level changes which may themselves have a climatic cause. On the other hand, Permian rocks from the same re- gion provided virtual pole positions whose dis- persion was surprisingly small. Irving and Parry (1963) have shown, the directions of magnetization of some Carboniferous rocks from Australia are similar to those found in Australian Permian rocks. To avoid confusion they went so far as to propose that an independent magnetic chronology be set up. The basins here studied are particularly apposite to the paleomagnetic study of the Carboniferous-Permian boundary, for there are lithologies suitable for paleomag- netic work, well dated because of the economic importance of the included coals. This time interval is not particularly well known paleo- magnetically (see, however, Creer and others 1959; Everitt and Belshe, 1960; Nairn, 1960; Collinson and Nairn, 1960). Until recently it has been generally assumed that relative movements within a continental block are unimportant, and one of the major problems has been to understand the dispersion of virtual pole positions found for some periods, such as the Carboniferous. The growing aware- ness of rotation of presumed tectonic origin, even within a continental area (Black, 1964; Kotasek and Krs, 1965; Ashworth and Nairn, 1965; Watkins, 1964; Irving and Opdyke, 1965; Kawai and others, 1962; van Hilten, 1962), necessitates the study of relatively re- stricted areas between which there are differ- ences in tectonic develop

ky Brod (Rossitz-Bohmische Brod). The nearly flat-lying sediments arc practically un- disturbed except by faulting, more marked in the Plzeii basin than in the Kladno basin. This reflects renewed activity along older tectonic lines until as late as the Tertiary. Sedimenta- tion occurred with only minor breaks (sec Table 1) until the end of the Stcphanian, with a maximum in Westphalian D and Stephanian B. The presence of Permian rocks has some- times been assumed (for example, Dorn, 1966), but has not been proven (see Havlena, 1966). The sedimentary rocks are predominantly continental sandstones and shales with eco- nomically important coal scams and some kaolin deposits. Volcanic rocks, porphyries, mclaphyres and tufls are known here as well as m the Inner Sudetic basin, and these may, as there, be related to weak movements of the Asturic phase. The (lows may show kaoliniza- tion, often taken as an indication of climate. The succession forms a sequence of alternating red and gray beds. This alternation has been attributed to climatic variation, but may equally well be due to fluctuating ground-water level consequent upon minor uplifts or depres- sions of tectonic origin, or to sea-level changes which may themselves have a climatic cause. and Southwest Center for Advanced Studies, Dallas, Texas, USA Received 28 February 1968 Late Jurassic-Early Cretaceous dolerites from Spitsbergen have normal and reversed directions of magnetization at low temperatures. After thermal demagnetization, all specimens are reversed. This reversed direction is interpreted as resulting from magnetization during a period of reversed field polarity. The dispersion in the directions of mag- netization after cleaning is attributed to incomplete removal of a secondary magnetization dominant at low tempera- tures. This secondary component is in part related to the magnetic properties of original titanomagnetite in the doler- ites, and in part to post-intrusion alteration. A weighted mean, computed from directions of magnetization which remain reversed, yields a paleomagnetic pole for the dolerites in the Atlantic region at 2.0°E, 60.1°N (6p = 16.1 °, 5m = 16"8°)" This is considerably removed from poles for other northern hemisphere rocks of the same age. 1. Our initial intention in sampling the Mississippian Maringouin beds of southeastern New Brunswick was to study this particular problem. The age of the Maringouin beds is considered to be late Mississippian (Weeks 1963). They are commonly cited as the oldest formation of the Hopewell Group, regarded as transitional from Mississippian to Pennsylvanian. Cornwell* (Received 1966 May 9) Summary The directions of magnetization and the magnetic properties of the Exeter lavas and the associated red sediments have been measured. The lavas have been placed in the Stephanian on the basis of recent age deter- minations (280 m.y.) but they are interbedded with the desert type sedi- ments typical of New Red Sandstone times in southwest England. The directions of the lavas generally show little scatter and are very resistant to both thermal and a.c. demagnetization. This is probably connected with the fact that their remanence is to a large extent due to haematite and a crystallization remanence (CRM). It is likely that the CRM was formed when the lavas were exposed to weathering soon after they were extruded in desert conditions. The palaeomagnetic pole position agrees with that established by an earlier investigation of the lavas. The associated sedi- ments are not altogether satisfactory for rock magnetic studies owing to their friable nature but yield a pole position similar to that of the lavas. 1. It seems likely that the magnetization of the haematite component is a crystalliza- tion remanence and was acquired when the magnetite was oxidized soon after the extrusion of the lavas in the New Red Sandstone desert of southwest England. The lack of correlation between the magnetic properties and the composition of the main series of lavas is presumably a result of the oxidation. All the lavas and sediments examined were magnetized near the palaeoequator in a field of opposite polarity to that existing at the present time. The continuous existence of a true reversed field during the Upper Carboniferous and Permian is indicated by numerous palaeomagnetic measurements on different continents. For the Exeter lavas the fact that similar directions were found for a wide variety of rock types and for two magnetic components from the same rock argues strongly against the existence of self-reversal mechanisms. The mean direction for all the lavas is 188" - 13" and the corresponding paleo- magnetic pole lies at 46" N and 165" E. This is certainly because the experimental difficulties encountered in the determination of field intensity from rocks and the uncertainties in the interpretation of the results obtained are much greater than in the corresponding measurements of direction only. IRVING Dominion Observatory, Ottawa, Canada Paleomagnetic observations have been obtained from 161 specimens from the Bloomsburg redbeds (Upper Silurian) collected at 13 localities along the tectonic arc in the Valley and Ridge province in the Appalachians. The purpose was to determine if the curvature was original, or if it was produced by bending in plan, during, say, the Appalachian orogeny. Observations were obtained from the eastern and southern limbs and from the hinge area of the arc. In the southern limb, in Maryland and Virginia, however, less stable secondary components probably of Permian age appear to have replaced much of the original magnetization, so that a rigorous test was un- fortunately not possible. Most of the cleaned southerly directions are like those in Permian rocks of West Virginia [Helsle.y, 1965] and eastern Canada [Roy, 1963b, 1966; Black, 1964]. Since this was the time in which the Bloomsburg beds were deformed (Appalachian orogeny), it is reasonable to suppose that the southerly magnetizations were acquired at that time, either by chemical change, by viscosity during a period of moderate heating at low temperatures (viscous PTRM as referred to by Chamalaun [1964]), or a combination of the two. Heating tests comparable to those made by Shimizu [1960] and Briden [1965] were made to investigate viscous PTRM effects. The procedure was to heat specimens at 300øC in the earth's field for periods of up to 3 weeks and then to measure the magnetization acquired in that time. To simplify the experiments only vertical components were measured. The ver- tical component of the applied field was 0.56 oe. This may not be a realistic modeling of condi- tions during burial, but the experiments give some indication of the effects likely to arise. An automatically controlled nonmagnetic fur- nace built at the Dominion Observatory was used. Its description is given here for the first time. to the fracture plane and would form ready pathways for ascending magmas. In the Appalachians the dike swarms are re- stricted to a zone trending NE-SW, following the main mountain axis. A pure-shear deforma- tion of such a zone by a stress directed from SE to NW can be expected to form primary tension fractures trending mostly NW-SE. If simple-shear deformation took place in a zone trending NE-SW, tension fractures can be ex- pected to cut that zone diagonally. These frac- tures originate at an angle of about 45 ø to the main shear plane (here supposedly trending more or less NE-SW); they will rotate syn- chronously with the polarity of the movements. If the rotational movements develop with a sinistral polarity, tension faults trending from about NNE to NNW can be expected; if the rotational movement develops with a dextral polarity, the trends would sway from ENE to WNW. The fan-shaped distribution of the Ap- palachian dike swarms does not fit either of these patterns. As in most mountain belts, the fracture system occupied by the dikes was most probably formed by a combination of pure- and simple-shear deformation. A possible explanation for the fan-shaped dike distribution may lie in a gradual change of the shear system in the NE-SW-trending crustal se

em in the north- east (see Figure 4). This requires a decrease BOER of the compressional component of the PH$ (the NW-SE component), and an increase of the rotational component of the PHS (the NE- SW component) in northeast direction. If we assume that the dike trends are indicative of the direction of PHS (in other words, that the dikes intruded first-order tension fractures), then the compressional movements dominated in the southwestern Appalachian segment and the rotational movements were more significant in the northeastern segment of the Appalachians. In this case we are dealing with a simple-shear system with sinistral polarity. Under conditions of predominant simple shear in the northeastern segment of the Appa- lachians, rotations of large-scale crustal units can be expected. Such rotations have actually been measured for Newfoundland. Black [1964] com- pared the late Paleozoic magnetic directions 6f rocks sampled there with those from New Brunswick and Quebec. Its deviating palcomag- netic poles as well as its varying structural trend indicate that Newfoundland has rotated counterclockwise about 30 ø with respect to the mainland, assuming the prevalence of simple- shear movements with sinistral polarity at the time of rotation. SUMMARY AND DISCUSSION The major part of the NRM in rock units investigated is primary, although secondary magnetic components have been added to out- crops of many rock units. Most of the secondary magnetization is believed to be iso- thermal reinanent magnetization (IRM) pro- duced by lightning; some secondary magneti- zation may be VRM acquired in the earth's field. Lightning-induced magnetization has been recognized by the localized occurrence of anomalous magnetization in isolated outcrops, by the general character of the outcrop terrain which in places includes lightning-struck nat- ural objects such as trees, and by the typical hardness of the magnetization which may ordi- narily be randomized in peak alternating fields of less than 450 oe. The virtual magnetic poles for the different geologic periods in Russia, western Europe, and England are given in Table 3. The virtual mag- netic poles of Russia, western Europe, and Eng- land during the late Paleozoic agree remarkably well, favoring the opinion that meso-Europe formed one stable block during this period. The deviation of the declination of the paleomagnetic directions in northeast Italy, Corsica, and northeast Spain are indicative of counterclockwise rotations. These rotations are thought to be related to the dextral shear movements mentioned above. They were caused by subsidiary left lateral shear which developed in the mobile zones bordering the primary dextral faults. Similar structural systems are found in the former Tethys areas of Turkey (Anatolia fault system) and northwest Africa (Atlas fault system). The deviation of the declination of the paleomagnetic directions in northeast Italy, Corsica, and northeast Spain are indicative of counterclockwise rotations. The deviation of the declination of the paleomagnetic directions in northeast Italy, Corsica, and northeast Spain are indicative of counterclockwise rotations. These rotations are thought to be related to the dextral shear movements mentioned above. They were caused by subsidiary left lateral shear which developed in the mobile zones bordering the primary dextral faults. Similar structural systems are found in the former Tethys areas of Turkey (Anatolia fault system) and northwest Africa (Atlas fault system). The main conclusion drawn from the paleomagnetic data is that the Tethys mobile belt was and still is a zone of primary dextral shear. Introduction. INTRODUCTION The Prince Edward Island red beds a re presently believed to have been deposited as ear ly as late Pennsylvanian or early Permian (Langston, 196 3) but the age of the uppermost of these beds has not been definitely established because no fossil remnant's have so far been found in them. The only known occurrence of igneous ro cks within these beds is that at the eastern tip of George Island (p a rt of Hog Island), Malpequ e Bay. These ro cks appear to have been injected as a sill into the red sandstones while the latter were still undistu rbed and apparently unconsolidated. As the age of the red sandstone in this area is somewhat uncertain, any information pertaining to the intrusive would be of geological interest. GEOLOGICAL SETTING Milligan ( 1949) described the igneous rock as a dyke that 11 ••• strikes in a gene ral NNW direction and dips eastward at about 15 degrees, though the contact is not clearly defined. The hanging-wall sandstones have been eroded away, but the remnants of the dyke appear to be at least 10 feet thick. 11 The fine-grained blackish part of the intrusive mass is an olivine basalt. RESULTS OF THE SYRIAN SAMPLES The directions of the N.R.M.‘s are plotted in Fig.SA. With the exception of SYR 8 all samples reveal a more or less similar characteristic magnet- ization in the process of dema~etization (Fig.9). The samples from the location near Saouda (SYR 1-4) yielded a rather remarkable result. At least three magnetic directions were found in the progressive demagnetization. A very soft component is already removed be- low an a.c. magnetic field of 100 Oe. A second is found between values of 100 and 1,000 Oe and a third between 1,000 and 3,000 Oe. This third we re- gard as a very hard secondary component as we found its direction conforms with the present-day local geomagnetic field (Fig.10). The second component is very consistent with the characteristic component of the samples SYR 5-7 and therefore also considered to be the characteristic magnetization (Fig.QC). The Lebznon, sit- uated at the northern extremity of the African R%t Valley system, presents abundant outcrops of relatively undizturbed Mesozoic rocks, mainly lime- stones of neritic to deep marine facies. INTRODUCTION It is common knowledge now that often different remanent magnetiza- tions exist together in rocks, so that generally the direction of their total n.r.m. (natural remanent magnetization) is a compound datum. Hence the magnetization directions of rock samples, which have neither been analysed in the modern way by means of a.c. or thermal demagnetization nor been subjected to other stability tests, are unreliable data. However, the paleomagnetic literature still contains many data from the days in which the research workers were not fully aware of this compli- cation. Particularly, now that these data are increasingly used as proofs for various theories, it is time that such data are tested, and if necessary, revised. Apart from indications of a comparatively small viscous component, the magnetization appeared stable, the changes in direction during demagnetization are given in Fig.6B. Only a single Curie point about 580 ° was observed. Thermomagnetic curves, of which two copies of the photographic record obtained are illustrated in Fig.7, were obtained using a Curie-Chevallier balance. They show a small shift in the Curie temperature in the cooling curve only a little greater than the thermal lag of the instrument and suggest that the ferromagnetic component must be close to pure magnetite. Susceptibility was measured in fields of the order of 20e using a susceptibility bridge (CoLLINSON et al., 1963).
